Hello, Mrs Jacobs. How are we doing today?
Okay, I suppose.
So I see here that you made the appointment because of recent weight loss. How much weight have you lost?
Approximately 10 kilograms in the past four months or so.
Okay, and I'm going to assume that this weight loss has not been intentional?
Oh no, I just haven't had much of an appetite, and I'm having an increasing issue with vomiting.
I see. And does your vomiting happen soon after eating?
No, it generally happens many hours after I have eaten.
And are you experiencing any other changes in your health?
Yes. I live alone in a two-floor house and I have noticed over the last month that my legs feel weak when I go up the stairs or walk up a small hill near my house.
And I remember you telling me that two years ago you were prescribed beta blockers or hypertension.
Are you still taking that medication?
Well, I stopped taking the beta blockers about four months ago.
Okay. Well, let's take a look at the investigations that you had done for this appointment.
So I see that urea is out of the normal range and quite a bit higher, which suggests dehydration.
That is to be expected because of the vomiting you just mentioned.
And look here, your sodium and potassium levels are lower than I would expect.
That is also likely due to the vomiting.
The low potassium levels also likely explain the weakness you have been feeling.
So you said that you vomit quite a bit of time after eating, correct?
Yes, that is correct. Several hours at least.
Hmm. I'm afraid everything points to obstruction to stomach outflow.
I can also hear a sloshing sound through my stethoscope,
which suggests the presence of gas and fluid that are trapped inside the stomach.
So things can't go out, so they are coming back up?
That's one way to look at it.
But what could be blocking the food from leaving my stomach? I mean, that sounds quite serious.
Unfortunately, I cannot tell what the cause is from these investigations.
If the problem is in my stomach, wouldn't I be having stomach pain?
Depending on the cause of the obstruction, there would not necessarily be abdominal pain.
So we will have to do a gastroscopy and biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and look for the cause of your problem.
We could be looking at a chronic gastric ulcer or a tumour in the pyloric antrum,
which is a part of your stomach near the bottom.
But because of the retained food in your stomach
we will need to wash out your stomach
to make sure we can see what is causing the obstruction
of the outflow tract of the stomach.

Not that I can remember. I mean, if it was, my GP certainly didn't say anything at all about it being high.
I can also see that you have retinal haemorrhages and papilledema.
This, along with what may be renal failure, points to accelerated hypertension.
The most important thing right now is to lower your blood pressure at a gradual rate over the next 24 hours.
Rapid reduction can be dangerous and can cause arterial thrombosis and problems in a number of organs.
I'm going to order an IV of antihypertensive drugs.
It is also necessary to control your fluid intake and keep you under observation for the onset of pulmonary oedema.
We may also need to put you on dialysis due to the problem with your kidneys.
Dialysis? I mean, are my kidney problems that serious?
Well, if we notice the development of a pulmonary oedema, dialysis will be necessary
because you will not respond to diuretics due to the problems with your kidneys.
As to the severity of your renal failure, we don't know yet if the renal failure is chronic or acute or a mixture of both.
The kidneys are being damaged by the hypertension, but at this point we don't know if they are chronically damaged or if there is some other undiagnosed renal disease.
We will also do a renal ultrasound, which is quick and non-invasive, to be sure about the size of your kidneys.
What will the size of my kidney tell you?
Well, kidney atrophy or shrunken kidney would indicate a damaged kidney.
And what about my vision? Is this vision loss permanent or long-term?
I don't think so. Your impaired visual acuity should recover completely.
And what about my kidney? If there is damage, is it permanent?
Again, we'll have to wait and see about that.
Your hypertension has been damaging your kidney function for several weeks now, so...

I'm going to take just a moment to explain a bit of the difference

Traditionally, dental procedures rely on preparation designs

This includes preparation features such as retention and resistance form as well as tooth reduction to meet the strength requirements of the restorative material instead of prioritising the preservation of intact tooth structure.
and the result of this is that the restored tooth has significant additional preparation
and a significantly higher chance of complications such as post-op pain, sensitivity, root canal

So today we have a special guest here to talk about innovations in the field of physiotherapy.
I would like to welcome Sally Fields, a physiotherapist working with the NHS.
Welcome Sally.
Thank you for having me. I'm so happy to be here today to share my passion with others.
So, before we get into innovations, I would like to talk about the role of physiotherapy
in a person's overall health. So, how can it contribute to the health of the population?
That's a very good question. Physiotherapy takes a whole-person approach to health and well-being.
So, with the population getting older and more people living with long-term conditions,
it is necessary to use physiotherapy to help patients manage long-term medical conditions
such as Parkinson's, asthma, cystic fibrosis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
Just to put the situation in perspective,
three out of every five people in the UK have a long-term condition.
Oh, interesting.
How is physiotherapy used to manage a disease like cystic fibrosis?
I would never have thought of physiotherapy being used for that type of condition.
In the case of cystic fibrosis, regular physical activity and physiotherapy-led exercise
help improve physical function, cardiovascular performance and muscle strength.
Exercise may also aid airway clearance,
blow the rate of lung function decline, contribute to an improved quality of life.
In general, physiotherapy helps to build resilience in patients by building their capacity to manage their own health.
And it also helps to enable people to regain maximum levels of mobility, function and independence following an accident or as they recover from an illness.
Another interesting aspect of physiotherapy is the way it can be tailored to meet individuals' personal goals.
Because physiotherapy requires a lot of commitment and effort on the part of the patient, establishing personal goals is very important
Yes, it is definitely important for patients to play an active role in the management of a long-term condition
Definitely, and that's why physiotherapists are starting to work alongside GPs
practice physiotherapists can help to assess diagnose treat prescribe medicines and as well
as manage patients needs this new model of care is part of a multi-pronged approach that has the
potential to address the immediate crisis in general practice as well as of course help deliver

What is the first innovation that you're going to talk to us about today?
Well, the first is robot-assisted physiotherapy. I will give a few examples of how it is used to
give you a better idea of its current role and future potential. So, loss of arm function is a
common problem after stroke and there are ongoing clinical trials to determine to what degree
robot-assisted training can help patients recover upper limb movement. So is the robot replacing a
physiotherapist? Not at all. Using robots allow the therapist to get a greater understanding of
the neuro-recovery process and also helps to build a rich stream of data that assists in ongoing
patient diagnosis and customisation of therapy.
Okay, I see. So can you give us an example of how it might work?
Of course. So during robot-assisted training, the stroke patient sits at a table facing a
computer screen and place their arm into the device. The therapist then asks the patient
to undertake some arm exercises, such as moving between targets on the computer screen.
If, let's say, the person is unable to move their arm, then the robot moves the patient's arm.
But if the patient is able to initiate the movement, the robot provides adjustable levels
of assistance to facilitate the person's arm movement, which helps the brain and arm to learn
to work together again. As I said earlier, the clinical trials are currently being done on this
type of robot-assisted physiotherapy, so there is a lot we still don't know about the potential
of this therapy. Another type of robotic-assisted therapy uses what is called an exosuit, which is a
robotic-powered exoskeleton used in people with weak or paralysed legs caused by stroke, spinal
cord injury, as well as other neurological conditions. An exoskeleton, so does that mean
it goes over the body of the patient. Exactly. It is placed over the legs to help with standing
and walking. Specifically, it uses battery-powered motors to drive the legs. So the way it works
when the patient is moving is as the person shifts their weight, sensors are activated
that initiate steps, which can help the patient to relearn step patterns and weight shifts.
